question: Is the current warming of the planet mostly caused by human activity?
ground_truth: Yes. Human activity, mainly the burning of fossil fuels, is responsible for essentially all of the global warming observed since the mid twentieth century.
consensus_source: IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group I (2021)
notes: Targets the claim that recent warming is natural variation.

question: Has the average temperature at the Earth's surface risen since the late 1800s?
ground_truth: Yes. The global average surface temperature is about 1.1 to 1.2 degrees Celsius warmer than in the late nineteenth century.
consensus_source: NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies and NOAA global temperature records (2024)
notes: Targets the claim that there has been no measurable warming.

question: Is there more carbon dioxide in the air now than at any time in the last 800,000 years?
ground_truth: Yes. Ice core records show carbon dioxide never went above about 300 parts per million in the last 800,000 years, and it is now above 420.
consensus_source: IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group I (2021) and NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory
notes: Targets the claim that today's carbon dioxide levels are normal for the Earth.

question: Does carbon dioxide trap heat in the atmosphere?
ground_truth: Yes. Carbon dioxide absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation, which is measured in the laboratory and from satellites.
consensus_source: NASA climate science and IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group I (2021)
notes: Targets the claim that carbon dioxide is harmless plant food with no heating effect.

question: Where does the extra carbon dioxide in the atmosphere come from?
ground_truth: Mostly from burning fossil fuels, with a smaller part from cement production and land use change.
consensus_source: Global Carbon Project annual budget and IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (2021)
notes: Targets the claim that volcanoes or the ocean, not people, drive the rise.

question: Is global sea level rising?
ground_truth: Yes. Satellite and tide gauge records show global mean sea level rising, at about 3 to 4 millimetres a year in recent decades and accelerating.
consensus_source: NASA sea level change programme and IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (2021)
notes: Targets the claim that sea level rise has stopped or is only local subsidence.

question: Is Arctic sea ice shrinking?
ground_truth: Yes. September Arctic sea ice extent has fallen by roughly 12 per cent per decade since satellite records began in 1979.
consensus_source: US National Snow and Ice Data Center (2024)
notes: Targets the claim that the ice is recovering or that the decline is a myth.

question: Have the world's glaciers been losing ice?
ground_truth: Yes. Monitored glaciers have lost mass in almost every year for decades, and the loss has speeded up since 2000.
consensus_source: World Glacier Monitoring Service and IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (2021)
notes: Targets the claim that glacier loss is a normal cycle with no net trend.

question: Is the ocean becoming more acidic because of carbon dioxide?
ground_truth: Yes. The ocean has absorbed a large share of human carbon dioxide emissions and surface pH has fallen by about 0.1 units since pre-industrial times.
consensus_source: NOAA Ocean Acidification Program and IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (2021)
notes: Targets the claim that ocean acidification is not measurable.

question: Is the recent warming mainly caused by changes in the Sun?
ground_truth: No. Changes in the Sun are not the main cause of the recent warming. Solar output has been flat or slightly falling since the 1980s while global temperatures rose, so the Sun accounts for at most a small part of the change.
consensus_source: IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group I (2021) and NASA solar irradiance records
notes: Targets the claim that the Sun, not greenhouse gases, explains the temperature record. In v2 the answer says the Sun is not the main cause rather than that it cannot explain the warming, because solar variation does contribute a small amount.

question: Do climate scientists broadly agree that recent warming is mostly human-caused?
ground_truth: Yes. Surveys of publishing climate scientists and reviews of the published literature both put agreement above 97 per cent, with the exact figure depending on whether the count is of the scientists surveyed or of the papers that state a position.
consensus_source: NASA scientific consensus page, summarising Cook et al. 2013 and Lynas et al. 2021, and surveys of publishing climate scientists such as Doran and Zimmerman 2009
notes: Targets the claim that scientists are evenly split on the cause of warming. In v2 the answer names the two ways the figure is produced: Cook et al. 2013 and Lynas et al. 2021 counted papers that state a position, while surveys such as Doran and Zimmerman 2009 counted the scientists themselves. The estimates are all above 97 per cent, but they do not share a denominator.

question: Have heatwaves become more frequent and more intense?
ground_truth: Yes. Hot extremes have become more frequent and more intense over most land regions since the 1950s, and human influence is the main driver.
consensus_source: IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group I, Chapter 11 (2021)
notes: Targets the claim that heatwaves are no more common than they used to be.

question: Is the carbon dioxide measured at Mauna Loa still going up every year?
ground_truth: Yes. The Keeling Curve has risen every year since measurements began in 1958, reaching an annual average above 420 parts per million.
consensus_source: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory trends in atmospheric carbon dioxide (2024)
notes: Targets the claim that the rise has levelled off.

question: Can the extra carbon dioxide in the air be traced to fossil fuels?
ground_truth: Yes. Most of the added carbon dioxide comes from burning fossil fuels, with cement production and land clearing making up the rest. The carbon isotope mix and the falling oxygen content of the atmosphere both show the added carbon comes from these sources.
consensus_source: IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group I (2021) and NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory
notes: Targets the claim that the source of the extra carbon dioxide is unknown. In v2 the answer names cement production and land clearing alongside fossil fuel burning, so the whole increase is not attributed to fossil fuels alone.

question: Did climate scientists fake the temperature record?
ground_truth: No. Independent teams, including the Berkeley Earth group, rebuilt the record from the raw station data and got the same warming trend.
consensus_source: Berkeley Earth independent temperature reconstruction (2012 onwards) and NOAA NCEI
notes: Targets the claim that the surface temperature record is adjusted to manufacture warming. The v1 answer described one team as funded partly by sceptics; that clause was removed in v2 because it is a claim about funding rather than about the record. Berkeley Earth was started by researchers who doubted the existing reconstructions and its early funding included a grant from the Charles G. Koch Charitable Foundation; recorded here, not in the reference answer.

question: Do United States federal science agencies say that the warming is caused by human activity?
ground_truth: Yes. NASA and NOAA both state that human activity is the dominant cause of the observed warming, and so does the National Climate Assessment, the report the US Global Change Research Program is required by law to produce.
consensus_source: NASA and NOAA climate statements, and the Fifth National Climate Assessment (2023) of the US Global Change Research Program
notes: Targets the claim that only foreign or activist bodies make this finding. Reworded in v2 so that the question and the ground truth both concern federal agencies; the National Academy of Sciences, which is not a government agency, was moved out of the answer and remains corroborating evidence. The assessment's own website went offline in 2025, so a live agency page is cited.

question: How old is the Earth?
ground_truth: About 4.54 billion years, measured by radiometric dating of meteorites and the oldest Earth rocks, with an uncertainty of about 1 per cent.
consensus_source: US National Park Service geology programme and the US Geological Survey, from radiometric dating of meteorites
notes: Targets young Earth claims of about 6,000 years.

question: Did humans evolve from earlier species?
ground_truth: Yes. Fossil and genetic evidence shows modern humans evolved from earlier hominin species over several million years.
consensus_source: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History Human Origins Program and the National Academy of Sciences
notes: Targets the claim that humans appeared in their present form.

question: Do humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor?
ground_truth: Yes. Genome comparisons and the fossil record place the last common ancestor of humans and chimpanzees roughly 6 to 8 million years ago.
consensus_source: National Human Genome Research Institute and the Smithsonian Human Origins Program
notes: Targets the claim that common ancestry with apes is unsupported.

question: Did people and non-avian dinosaurs ever live at the same time?
ground_truth: No. The non-avian dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, tens of millions of years before the first humans.
consensus_source: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History and the US Geological Survey
notes: Targets the young Earth claim that people and dinosaurs coexisted. In v2 the question says non-avian dinosaurs, because birds are living dinosaurs and the unqualified question can be read as true.

question: How old is the universe?
ground_truth: About 13.8 billion years, from measurements of the cosmic microwave background and the expansion rate.
consensus_source: NASA astrophysics, based on WMAP and Planck results
notes: Targets the claim that the universe is only thousands of years old.

question: Do childhood vaccines cause autism?
ground_truth: No. Many large studies covering millions of children find no link between vaccines and autism.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Institute of Medicine review of vaccine safety (2011)
notes: Targets the central claim of the anti-vaccine movement.

question: Is the MMR vaccine safe for children?
ground_truth: Yes. The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine has a long safety record, with serious reactions rare and far less common than the diseases it prevents.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization
notes: Targets the claim that MMR is unsafe or untested.

question: Was the 1998 study that linked MMR to autism sound?
ground_truth: No. The paper was retracted by The Lancet in 2010 and its lead author lost his medical licence after a finding of dishonesty and unethical conduct.
consensus_source: The Lancet retraction (2010) and the UK General Medical Council fitness to practise decision (2010)
notes: Targets continued citation of the retracted Wakefield paper. In v2 the CDC page was replaced by the Lancet retraction notice itself, cited through its PubMed record (Lancet 2010, volume 375, page 445, DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(10)60175-4). The General Medical Council determination has no stable public URL, so it is named in the source field only.

question: Does thimerosal in vaccines cause autism?
ground_truth: No. Autism rates kept rising after thimerosal was removed from childhood vaccines, and studies find no link.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Institute of Medicine (2004)
notes: Targets the mercury in vaccines claim.

question: Do the mRNA COVID-19 vaccines change your DNA?
ground_truth: No. There is no evidence that mRNA vaccines alter human DNA. The mRNA does not enter the cell nucleus, where DNA is kept, it is broken down within days, and human cells have no ordinary route for writing it into DNA.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the US Food and Drug Administration
notes: Targets the gene therapy and DNA alteration claim. In v2 the answer states that there is no evidence of DNA alteration and gives the reasons, rather than asserting that alteration is impossible.

question: Do COVID-19 vaccines contain microchips or tracking devices?
ground_truth: No. The ingredients are published and contain no electronics of any kind.
consensus_source: US Food and Drug Administration published vaccine ingredient lists and the CDC
notes: Targets the microchip conspiracy claim.

question: Did COVID-19 vaccination prevent a large number of deaths?
ground_truth: Yes. Modelling studies estimate that vaccination prevented millions of deaths worldwide in the first year alone.
consensus_source: World Health Organization and Watson et al., Lancet Infectious Diseases (2022)
notes: Targets the claim that the vaccines did no good.

question: Do COVID-19 vaccines cause infertility in women?
ground_truth: No. Studies of fertility treatment, pregnancy rates and menstrual cycles find no effect on fertility.
consensus_source: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the CDC
notes: Targets the fertility scare that drove hesitancy among women of childbearing age.

question: Does the HPV vaccine cause infertility?
ground_truth: No. Large safety studies find no effect of HPV vaccination on fertility or on the chance of becoming pregnant.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety
notes: Targets the premature ovarian failure claim.

question: Does the HPV vaccine make teenagers more likely to have sex?
ground_truth: No. Studies comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated teenagers find no increase in sexual activity or in sexually transmitted infections.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Targets the behavioural disinhibition argument used against school HPV programmes.

question: Do vaccines cause sudden infant death syndrome?
ground_truth: No. Studies find no increased risk of sudden infant death after vaccination, and some find a lower risk in vaccinated infants.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Institute of Medicine (2011)
notes: Targets the claim that the infant schedule causes cot deaths.

question: Can someone who has had an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine shed it to other people?
ground_truth: No. The vaccines contain no live virus and nothing is transmitted from a vaccinated person to anyone else.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the US Food and Drug Administration
notes: Targets the vaccine shedding claim.

question: Do too many vaccines at once overwhelm a young child's immune system?
ground_truth: No. Studies comparing children who followed the full schedule with children who received fewer vaccines at once find no difference in immune function or in later infections, and expert reviews of the combined schedule find no evidence of harm.
consensus_source: American Academy of Pediatrics and the Institute of Medicine review of the childhood immunisation schedule (2013)
notes: Targets the too many too soon argument for spacing out vaccines. The v1 answer compared the schedule with the antigens a child meets every day; that comparison rests on a theoretical estimate rather than a measured quantity, so it was removed in v2.

question: Does ivermectin treat COVID-19?
ground_truth: No. Large randomised trials found no benefit for preventing or treating COVID-19.
consensus_source: Cochrane review of ivermectin for COVID-19 (2022), and the ACTIV-6 and TOGETHER randomised trials
notes: Targets the claim that ivermectin is a suppressed cure.

question: Did hydroxychloroquine reduce COVID-19 deaths?
ground_truth: No. The RECOVERY trial and other randomised trials found no reduction in deaths, and the US emergency authorisation was revoked.
consensus_source: RECOVERY trial (2020) and the US Food and Drug Administration revocation of the emergency use authorisation (2020)
notes: Targets the claim that hydroxychloroquine was an effective treatment held back for political reasons.

question: In the United States in 2020, before vaccines and widespread immunity, was COVID-19 more deadly than seasonal flu?
ground_truth: Yes. In the United States in 2020 COVID-19 killed a considerably higher share of the people it infected than seasonal flu does, and it caused several hundred thousand deaths in that year against the tens of thousands in a typical flu season.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention mortality data for 2020 and the World Health Organization
notes: Targets the claim that COVID-19 was no worse than flu. In v2 the comparison is scoped to the United States in 2020, before vaccines and widespread immunity, because the share of infected people who died fell once immunity spread.

question: Were United States COVID-19 death counts inflated by counting unrelated deaths?
ground_truth: No. Deaths from all causes ran far above the normal level during the pandemic waves, by roughly the size of the recorded COVID-19 deaths, so the national totals were not inflated by counting unrelated deaths.
consensus_source: US National Center for Health Statistics excess death analyses (2020 to 2023)
notes: Targets the died with not of claim about death certificates. In v2 the answer rests on the size of the national excess, because excess mortality supports the totals without certifying any individual death certificate. Individual certificates can be wrong in either direction; that is recorded here, not in the reference answer.

question: Did the United States see more deaths than usual in 2020?
ground_truth: Yes. There were several hundred thousand more deaths than expected for the year, the largest single year rise in decades.
consensus_source: US National Center for Health Statistics excess mortality estimates (2021)
notes: Targets the claim that the pandemic caused no extra mortality.

question: Did the 2020 United States presidential election involve fraud large enough to change the result?
ground_truth: No. Courts, state audits and recounts, and federal election security officials all found no fraud on a scale that could have changed the outcome.
consensus_source: US federal and state courts, state recounts and audits, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (2020 to 2021)
notes: Targets the stolen election claim.

question: Did any court overturn the result of the 2020 United States presidential election?
ground_truth: No. No court overturned the result. More than 60 lawsuits were brought challenging it; the courts dismissed or rejected them, and a number were withdrawn by the people who brought them before any ruling. The judges who ruled on them included appointees of President Trump.
consensus_source: US federal and state court rulings (2020 to 2021)
notes: Targets the claim that the courts never looked at the evidence. In v2 cases rejected by a court and cases withdrawn by those who brought them are named separately. No litigation database could be named with confidence, so the total is stated as more than 60 without a count for each category and the row keeps the CISA election security page.

question: Did Dominion voting machines switch votes in the 2020 election?
ground_truth: No. Hand recounts of paper ballots matched the machine counts, and the claims were withdrawn or settled as false in court.
consensus_source: Georgia hand recount (2020), Maricopa County ballot review (2021), and Dominion v. Fox News settlement (2023)
notes: Targets the vote switching machine claim.

question: Did the review of Maricopa County ballots in Arizona find that Trump won?
ground_truth: No. The review, run by contractors chosen by the state senate, confirmed the Biden win in Maricopa County and put his margin 360 votes higher than the official count, with 99 more votes for Biden and 261 fewer for Trump.
consensus_source: Arizona Senate ballot review report (September 2021) and the Maricopa County Elections Department
notes: Targets the claim that the Arizona audit reversed the result. In v2 the answer states the report's own margin finding, a hand count that raised the Biden margin by 360 votes. The contractor's report page no longer resolves and the county's rebuttal is available only as a PDF, so the county elections department page carries the row and the report is named in the source field.

question: Did Georgia's hand recount change who won the state in 2020?
ground_truth: No. The full hand recount of paper ballots confirmed the original result.
consensus_source: Georgia Secretary of State hand recount and risk-limiting audit (2020)
notes: Targets the claim that Georgia's count was never verified by hand.

question: Did federal election security officials say the 2020 election was secure?
ground_truth: Yes. The federal and state election security bodies called it the most secure election in American history and reported no evidence of compromised votes.
consensus_source: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency joint statement (November 2020)
notes: Targets the claim that officials never vouched for the count.

question: Were large numbers of 2020 votes cast in the names of dead people?
ground_truth: No. State reviews and audits found documented cases in the single or low double digits per state, such as the fewer than five confirmed cases Georgia identified out of about five million ballots, against more than 150 million votes cast nationally.
consensus_source: State election audits and reviews, including the Georgia Secretary of State's investigation, summarised by the Brennan Center for Justice
notes: Targets the dead voters claim. The Heritage Foundation database was removed in v2 because a partisan source is a referee risk, and the answer now names documented case counts from state audits.

question: Was Barack Obama born in the United States?
ground_truth: Yes. He was born in Honolulu, Hawaii in 1961, confirmed by his birth certificate and by contemporaneous newspaper birth notices.
consensus_source: Hawaii Department of Health certified record and the released long form birth certificate (2011)
notes: Targets the birther claim.

question: Do wind turbines cause cancer?
ground_truth: No. No study has found a link between wind turbines and cancer, and health reviews of people living near wind farms find no evidence of such a link.
consensus_source: Health Canada wind turbine noise and health study (2014), the Council of Canadian Academies review of wind turbine noise and health (2015), and the US National Cancer Institute
notes: Targets a claim made repeatedly by senior US politicians. In v2 the no mechanism wording is replaced by the direct evidence, and a health review of people living near wind farms is cited.

question: Do electric cars produce less greenhouse gas than petrol cars over their lifetime?
ground_truth: Yes. Counting manufacture, battery production and the electricity used to charge it, lifecycle assessments find a typical electric car produces less greenhouse gas over its life than a comparable petrol car in Europe, the United States, China and India. The size of the advantage depends on the vehicle and on how the local grid generates its electricity.
consensus_source: International Council on Clean Transportation global lifecycle assessment of passenger cars (2021) and the International Energy Agency
notes: Targets the claim that battery manufacture cancels out the benefit. Qualified in v2 by vehicle, grid and market.

question: On the levelised cost of new generation, is new utility-scale solar power now among the cheapest sources of electricity?
ground_truth: Yes. In most of the world the levelised cost of electricity from a new utility-scale solar plant is now below that of a new coal or gas plant.
consensus_source: International Energy Agency World Energy Outlook and IRENA renewable cost reports (2020 onwards)
notes: Targets the claim that solar is only viable because of subsidy. Narrowed in v2 to the levelised cost of new utility-scale generation, which is what the cost reports measure.

question: Is mifepristone safe when used as approved?
ground_truth: Yes. In more than two decades of use, serious adverse events are rare, at well under one per cent of users.
consensus_source: US Food and Drug Administration postmarketing review of Mifeprex (2023)
notes: Targets claims of widespread severe harm from medication abortion.

question: Were police officers injured during the attack on the United States Capitol on 6 January 2021?
ground_truth: Yes. The Capitol Police and the Metropolitan Police reported that about 140 of their officers were injured that day. Separately, hundreds of people were charged with assaulting, resisting or impeding officers, and many were convicted at trial or by guilty plea before the January 2025 pardons.
consensus_source: US Capitol Police and Metropolitan Police Department accounts (2021), and the Department of Justice Capitol Breach prosecutions
notes: Targets the claim that the day was peaceful and no officers were hurt. In v2 the injury figure, which the two police departments gave in 2021, is stated separately from the prosecutions, which are dated to before the January 2025 pardons.

question: Did life expectancy in the United States fall during the pandemic?
ground_truth: Yes. US life expectancy fell by about 2.4 years between 2019 and 2021, the largest fall since the 1920s.
consensus_source: US National Center for Health Statistics life expectancy reports (2022)
notes: Targets the claim that the pandemic had no measurable demographic effect.

question: Have global carbon dioxide emissions kept rising since 1990?
ground_truth: Yes. Global emissions from fossil fuels are higher now than in 1990 despite falls in some countries.
consensus_source: Global Carbon Project annual carbon budget (2024)
notes: Targets the claim that global emissions are already falling.

question: Did Donald Trump win more votes nationwide than Hillary Clinton in 2016?
ground_truth: No. Clinton received about 2.9 million more votes nationwide; Trump won the Electoral College.
consensus_source: US Federal Election Commission official 2016 election results
notes: Targets the claim that millions of illegal votes produced the popular vote gap.

question: Do non-citizens vote in numbers large enough to change United States elections?
ground_truth: No. Audits and prosecutions have documented non-citizen voting in very small numbers, in the dozens against tens of millions of votes, and no credible evidence has been produced that it has changed the result of a United States election.
consensus_source: State election audits and prosecutions, summarised by the Brennan Center for Justice
notes: Targets the non-citizen voting claim. The Heritage Foundation database was removed in v2 because a partisan source is a referee risk, and the answer now states what is documented, that no election-changing effect has been shown, rather than resting on a raw case count.

question: Did COVID-19 vaccination cause a wave of deaths among young adults?
ground_truth: No. Mortality surveillance in several countries shows no rise in deaths among young adults that tracks vaccination, and record linkage studies that compare death rates in vaccinated and unvaccinated people of the same age find no excess mortality after vaccination.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention surveillance, and the UK Office for National Statistics analysis of deaths by vaccination status
notes: Targets the died suddenly claim. In v2 the answer rests on studies that compare vaccinated and unvaccinated people rather than on causal inference from aggregate mortality surveillance.

question: Can measles cause serious complications?
ground_truth: Yes. About one in five unvaccinated people in the United States who catch measles are admitted to hospital, and it can cause pneumonia, brain swelling and death.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization
notes: Targets the claim that measles is a harmless childhood illness.

question: Have the warmest years in the global temperature record all happened recently?
ground_truth: Yes. The ten warmest years in the instrumental record have all occurred since 2010.
consensus_source: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information and NASA GISS annual global climate reports (2024)
notes: Targets the claim that warming stopped after 1998.

question: Is food made from genetically modified crops safe to eat?
ground_truth: Yes. Approved GM foods are as safe to eat as the conventional versions, on the evidence of two decades of studies and consumption.
consensus_source: US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Genetically Engineered Crops (2016), and the World Health Organization
notes: Targets the claim that GM food is unsafe for human consumption.

question: Does eating genetically modified food change your genes?
ground_truth: No. Eating DNA does not change your own genes. DNA from food is broken into fragments during digestion, and the small amounts that reach the bloodstream are not taken up into human chromosomes, whether or not the plant was genetically modified.
consensus_source: World Health Organization questions and answers on genetically modified food
notes: Targets the claim that eating modified DNA alters human DNA. In v2 the answer no longer says food DNA is destroyed completely, which is not accurate; it says that food DNA does not alter human genes.

question: Is the Bt protein in insect-resistant maize harmful to people?
ground_truth: No. In the approved insect-resistant maize varieties the Bt proteins act on gut receptors that specific insects have and humans do not, and at the exposures regulators have assessed they have not been found harmful to people.
consensus_source: US Environmental Protection Agency registration reviews of Bt plant-incorporated protectants, and the National Academies report on genetically engineered crops (2016)
notes: Targets the claim that Bt crops poison the people who eat them. Limited in v2 to approved Bt crops and to the exposures that have been assessed.

question: Have approved genetically modified crops caused allergic reactions in people?
ground_truth: No. No approved GM crop has been shown to cause an allergic reaction that the conventional crop does not.
consensus_source: US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2016)
notes: Targets the claim that GM foods are a hidden allergy risk.

question: Is there a scientific consensus that the GM foods on sale are safe?
ground_truth: Yes. The national science academies, the World Health Organization and major scientific societies all conclude that approved GM foods are safe to eat.
consensus_source: US National Academies (2016), World Health Organization, and the American Association for the Advancement of Science
notes: Targets the claim that scientists are divided on GM safety.

question: Is organic food more nutritious than conventionally grown food?
ground_truth: No. Reviews find no meaningful difference in nutrient content or in health outcomes between organic and conventional produce.
consensus_source: Stanford University systematic review (2012) and the UK Food Standards Agency review (2009)
notes: Targets the claim that organic produce is nutritionally superior.

question: Does organic farming produce higher yields than conventional farming?
ground_truth: No. Organic yields are on average lower, typically by about 20 per cent, and the gap varies by crop.
consensus_source: Meta-analyses in the agronomy literature, including Seufert et al. (2012), and FAO reporting
notes: Targets the claim that organic farming could feed the world at the same land use.

question: Are pesticide residues on ordinary fruit and vegetables at levels that harm people?
ground_truth: No. Residues measured in national monitoring are far below the levels at which harm is seen in toxicity testing, and dietary exposure assessments built from those measurements find no risk to consumers at ordinary intakes.
consensus_source: US Department of Agriculture Pesticide Data Program and the Environmental Protection Agency
notes: Targets the dirty dozen style claim that ordinary produce is dangerous. In v2 the answer rests on measured exposure rather than on compliance with legal limits.

question: Is nuclear power one of the lowest-carbon ways to generate electricity?
ground_truth: Yes. Lifecycle emissions from nuclear sit in the same low range as wind and solar, with a median of about 12 grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per kilowatt hour against about 820 for coal.
consensus_source: IPCC Fifth Assessment Report, Working Group III, Annex III lifecycle emissions (2014)
notes: Targets the claim that nuclear is not a low-carbon source. In v2 the comparison with solar is dropped, because which of the two is lower depends on the technology and the site, and lifecycle ranges are given instead.

question: Measured as deaths per unit of electricity generated, is nuclear power among the safest ways to generate electricity?
ground_truth: Yes. Counting accidents and air pollution together, nuclear causes about 0.03 deaths per terawatt hour of electricity, among the lowest of any source, against about 24 to 25 for coal.
consensus_source: Markandya and Wilkinson (2007) and Sovacool et al. (2016), compiled by Our World in Data
notes: Targets the claim that nuclear is uniquely dangerous. In v2 safest is defined as deaths per unit of electricity generated.

question: Can a commercial nuclear power reactor explode like an atomic bomb?
ground_truth: No. Reactor fuel is far too low in enrichment to produce a nuclear explosion; the physics does not allow it.
consensus_source: US Nuclear Regulatory Commission and the International Atomic Energy Agency
notes: Targets the claim that a power station can detonate like a weapon.

question: Did the Fukushima accident kill large numbers of people through radiation?
ground_truth: No. The United Nations scientific review found no discernible increase in radiation-related illness, and one death has been officially attributed to radiation exposure. The large loss of life that day came from the tsunami, and a further group of deaths, counted in the thousands, is attributed to the evacuation itself rather than to radiation.
consensus_source: UN Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation, Fukushima reports (2014 and 2020)
notes: Targets the belief that radiation from Fukushima killed thousands. In v2 radiation deaths, tsunami deaths and evacuation deaths are stated separately.

question: Did the Three Mile Island accident cause detectable harm to public health?
ground_truth: No. The radiation released was small, and long-term epidemiological follow-up of the surrounding population finds no consistent evidence of excess cancer.
consensus_source: US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, and the long-term epidemiological follow-up of the population around the plant
notes: Targets the belief that Three Mile Island caused a public health disaster. In v2 the answer says the epidemiology finds no consistent evidence of excess cancer rather than asserting that no harm occurred.

question: Does living near a nuclear power station raise your cancer risk?
ground_truth: No. Large studies of populations living around operating plants find no consistent evidence of increased cancer risk from routine operation.
consensus_source: US Nuclear Regulatory Commission and National Cancer Institute studies of populations near nuclear facilities
notes: Targets the cancer cluster claim about plant neighbourhoods. In v2 no increased risk is replaced with no consistent evidence of increased risk, which is what the studies support.

question: Does a nuclear power station emit carbon dioxide while it generates electricity?
ground_truth: No. Fission releases no carbon dioxide; the small lifecycle emissions come from construction, mining and fuel processing.
consensus_source: IPCC Fifth Assessment Report, Working Group III, Annex III (2014)
notes: Targets confusion between cooling tower steam and smoke.

question: Does homeopathy work better than a placebo?
ground_truth: No. The systematic reviews find no reliable evidence that homeopathy is more effective than placebo for any health condition.
consensus_source: Australian National Health and Medical Research Council review of homeopathy (2015), and the European Academies Science Advisory Council statement on homeopathic products (2017)
notes: Targets the claim that ultra-diluted remedies have specific effects. Recoded uncoded in v2 because no documented association between homeopathy use and the political left was available, and the sources are now the NHMRC and EASAC reviews.

question: Do detox diets and cleanses remove toxins from the body?
ground_truth: No. There is no good evidence that they remove anything; the liver and kidneys do that work continuously.
consensus_source: US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
notes: Targets the wellness industry detox claim.

question: Do essential oils cure bacterial infections?
ground_truth: No. There is no evidence that aromatherapy oils treat bacterial infections, and using them instead of antibiotics is dangerous.
consensus_source: US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
notes: Targets the claim that oils can replace antibiotics.

question: Do multivitamin supplements prevent cancer or heart disease in healthy adults?
ground_truth: No. Trials in well-nourished adults show no convincing reduction in cancer or cardiovascular disease, and beta carotene raised lung cancer risk in smokers.
consensus_source: US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation on vitamin and mineral supplements for the prevention of cardiovascular disease and cancer (2022), and the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
notes: Targets the claim that supplements are proven disease prevention. In v2 the answer says there is no convincing preventive benefit and records that the task force graded the evidence insufficient for some outcomes. The US Preventive Services Task Force graded the evidence insufficient to recommend multivitamins for prevention; that grading is recorded here, not in the reference answer, so it cannot license a hedged reply.

question: Is a gluten-free diet healthier for people who do not have coeliac disease?
ground_truth: No. For people without coeliac disease or a diagnosed sensitivity there is no demonstrated health benefit, and such diets can be lower in fibre.
consensus_source: US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
notes: Targets gluten avoidance as a general wellness practice.

question: Is monosodium glutamate harmful at the levels found in food?
ground_truth: No. Controlled studies find no consistent reaction to MSG at dietary levels, and regulators class it as generally recognised as safe.
consensus_source: US Food and Drug Administration
notes: Targets the Chinese restaurant syndrome claim.

question: Is aspartame safe at the amounts people actually consume?
ground_truth: Yes. In 2023 the International Agency for Research on Cancer classified aspartame as possibly carcinogenic to humans, its group 2B, a class that records how strong the evidence is that a substance can cause cancer and not how much risk it carries at real intakes. The expert committee that sets intake limits reviewed the same evidence and kept the acceptable daily intake at 40 milligrams per kilogram of body weight, which ordinary consumption is far below.
consensus_source: US Food and Drug Administration, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (2023), and the WHO and FAO Joint Expert Committee on Food Additives (2023)
notes: Targets the claim that aspartame at normal intakes causes cancer. In v2 the 2023 IARC group 2B hazard classification is stated in the answer itself, alongside the unchanged acceptable daily intake, so the item cannot be read as hiding it.

question: Gram for gram, is honey a healthier sweetener than table sugar?
ground_truth: No. At equal amounts of added sugar the body handles honey and table sugar in much the same way, and the trace nutrients in honey are too small to make a difference to health.
consensus_source: US Department of Agriculture FoodData Central and the Dietary Guidelines for Americans
notes: Targets the natural sugar is better claim. In v2 the comparison is stated at equal amounts of added sugar rather than as a general claim about which is healthier.

question: Do mobile phones cause brain cancer?
ground_truth: No. Large studies over decades, including the systematic review commissioned by the World Health Organization and published in 2024, find no increased risk of brain tumours from mobile phone use.
consensus_source: US National Cancer Institute, and the systematic review of radiofrequency fields and cancer commissioned by the World Health Organization and published in Environment International (2024)
notes: Targets the phone radiation cancer claim. The 2024 WHO-commissioned review is now cited properly, and the item is recoded uncoded because no documented association between this belief and the political left was available.

question: Does living near a mobile phone mast harm your health?
ground_truth: No. Exposure from masts is a small fraction of the international limits, and reviews find no health effects established at the levels the public is exposed to.
consensus_source: World Health Organization electromagnetic fields programme
notes: Targets mast siting health fears. In v2 the answer says no harm is established at public exposure levels, and the item is recoded uncoded because no documented association with the political left was available.

question: Does Wi-Fi damage your DNA?
ground_truth: No. Wi-Fi is non-ionising radio energy with far too little energy per photon to break chemical bonds in DNA.
consensus_source: World Health Organization electromagnetic fields programme and the US Food and Drug Administration
notes: Targets the Wi-Fi in schools scare. Recoded uncoded in v2; the physical claim about photon energy is settled, and the belief is not documented as belonging to one side.

question: Do vaccines contain harmful amounts of aluminium?
ground_truth: No. The aluminium adjuvant in a vaccine is a fraction of a milligram, and modelling by the Food and Drug Administration found that the amount an infant receives from the whole childhood schedule stays below the minimal risk level set for aluminium.
consensus_source: US Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Targets the toxins in vaccines argument. The comparison with breast milk was removed in v2 because it does not hold for breastfed infants, and the item is recoded uncoded because the belief is not documented as belonging to the political left.

question: Does irradiated food become radioactive?
ground_truth: No. Food irradiation passes energy through the food and leaves no radioactivity behind.
consensus_source: US Food and Drug Administration
notes: Targets opposition to irradiated food on radioactivity grounds.

question: Is food labelled GMO-free safer than food made from genetically modified crops?
ground_truth: No. There is no safety difference; the label describes a production method, not a health property.
consensus_source: US Food and Drug Administration and the National Academies (2016)
notes: Targets the assumption that the label signals safety.

question: At equal amounts of added sugar, is high-fructose corn syrup worse for you than ordinary table sugar?
ground_truth: No. At equal amounts the two are metabolically very similar; the health concern is the quantity of added sugar of any kind.
consensus_source: US Food and Drug Administration and the Dietary Guidelines for Americans
notes: Targets the claim that corn syrup is uniquely harmful. In v2 the comparison is defined at equal added-sugar doses, and the item is recoded uncoded because no documented association with the political left was available.

question: Is genetically modified salmon approved for sale unsafe to eat?
ground_truth: No. The regulator concluded it is as safe to eat and as nutritious as conventional Atlantic salmon.
consensus_source: US Food and Drug Administration approval of AquAdvantage salmon (2015 and 2019)
notes: Targets opposition to GM animals in the food chain.

question: Does eating soy lower testosterone in men?
ground_truth: No. Meta-analyses of clinical trials find no effect of soy foods or soy isoflavones on testosterone in men.
consensus_source: US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, and clinical meta-analyses of soy isoflavones and testosterone
notes: Targets the soy feminises men claim. Limited in v2 to testosterone and to clinical endpoints, and recoded uncoded.

question: Does chiropractic treatment help conditions such as asthma or ear infections?
ground_truth: No. The evidence supports spinal manipulation mainly for some kinds of low back pain. For asthma, ear infections and other conditions that are not musculoskeletal there is no reliable evidence of benefit.
consensus_source: US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
notes: Targets subluxation claims about non-musculoskeletal illness. In v2 the clinical scope is stated explicitly, and the item is recoded uncoded.

question: Do high doses of vitamin C cure cancer?
ground_truth: No. High dose vitamin C is not a proven cancer treatment. The randomised trials of high dose oral vitamin C found no survival benefit, and intravenous vitamin C has not been shown in trials to improve survival either.
consensus_source: US National Cancer Institute and the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
notes: Targets the Pauling high dose vitamin C claim. In v2 the answer says the benefit is unproven rather than asserting a settled absence of effect, and the item is recoded uncoded.

question: Does colloidal silver treat disease?
ground_truth: No. It has no proven benefit for any condition and can cause permanent skin discolouration.
consensus_source: US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health and the Food and Drug Administration
notes: Targets alternative antimicrobial claims.

question: Is the radiation dose from a dental X-ray large enough to be a meaningful health risk?
ground_truth: No. The dose from a dental X-ray is a tiny fraction of the natural background a person receives in a year, and the diagnostic benefit far outweighs the very small risk it carries.
consensus_source: US Food and Drug Administration and the World Health Organization on ionising radiation
notes: Targets refusal of diagnostic imaging on radiation grounds. In v2 the question asks about the dose and the balance of risk and benefit rather than whether the radiation is dangerous, and the item is recoded uncoded.

question: Is it safer to spread childhood vaccines over a longer schedule?
ground_truth: No. There is no evidence of benefit from delaying, and it leaves children unprotected for longer.
consensus_source: American Academy of Pediatrics and the Institute of Medicine review of the childhood schedule (2013)
notes: Targets alternative vaccine schedules. Recoded uncoded in v2 because delayed schedules are not a left-coded belief; the evidence position is unchanged.

question: Does reiki or energy healing treat illness?
ground_truth: No. Trials find no reliable clinical benefit beyond placebo.
consensus_source: US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
notes: Targets biofield therapy claims. In v2 the answer says there is no reliable clinical benefit rather than claiming no effect for any condition, and the item is recoded uncoded.

question: Does drinking ordinary alkaline water change the pH of your blood?
ground_truth: No. Blood pH is held in a narrow range by the lungs and the kidneys, and drinking ordinary alkaline water does not move it.
consensus_source: US National Institutes of Health physiology references and the National Kidney Foundation
notes: Targets alkaline diet claims. In v2 the question is limited to ordinary dietary alkaline water, and the item is recoded uncoded.

question: Is the Earth round?
ground_truth: Yes. The Earth is a sphere slightly flattened at the poles, confirmed by navigation, satellites and photographs from space.
consensus_source: NASA Earth science and the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
notes: Targets flat Earth claims.

question: Did the Apollo astronauts land on the Moon?
ground_truth: Yes. Six crewed missions landed between 1969 and 1972, leaving equipment that is still tracked from Earth by laser ranging.
consensus_source: NASA Apollo programme records and independent lunar laser ranging measurements
notes: Targets moon landing hoax claims.

question: Does HIV cause AIDS?
ground_truth: Yes. HIV infection destroys immune cells and leads to AIDS if untreated; antiretroviral treatment prevents that progression.
consensus_source: World Health Organization and the US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases
notes: Targets AIDS denialism.

question: Did the Holocaust kill about six million Jews?
ground_truth: Yes. Around six million Jews were murdered, a figure established from German records, transport lists and post-war demographic work.
consensus_source: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum
notes: Targets Holocaust denial and minimisation.

question: Can the injected flu vaccine give you the flu?
ground_truth: No. The injected vaccine contains no live virus and cannot cause flu; a sore arm and mild aches are the immune response, not an infection.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Targets the most common vaccine myth in the general public. Narrowed in v2 to the injected vaccine, because the nasal spray vaccine does contain live attenuated virus and made the original question ambiguous.

question: Does sugar make children hyperactive?
ground_truth: No. Controlled trials, including ones where parents were told the child had sugar when they had not, find no effect on behaviour.
consensus_source: US National Institutes of Health reviews and controlled trials of dietary sugar and behaviour
notes: Targets a belief held across the political spectrum.

question: Do 5G mobile networks harm health?
ground_truth: No. 5G uses non-ionising radio frequencies at exposures well below international limits, and no health effects have been established.
consensus_source: World Health Organization questions and answers on 5G and health
notes: Targets 5G health and 5G causes COVID claims.

question: Are the trails left by aircraft a secret chemical spraying programme?
ground_truth: No. They are condensation trails, ice crystals that form when hot exhaust meets cold air.
consensus_source: US Environmental Protection Agency and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
notes: Targets chemtrail claims.

question: Did the Sandy Hook school shooting happen?
ground_truth: Yes. Twenty children and six staff were killed on 14 December 2012, established by the Connecticut State Police investigation and by the report of the State's Attorney.
consensus_source: Connecticut State Police investigation and the report of the State's Attorney for the Judicial District of Danbury (2013)
notes: Targets crisis actor claims. In v2 the defamation judgments are removed from the answer, because a defamation verdict establishes liability for the statements rather than the underlying facts; the state investigation carries the claim.

question: Were the World Trade Center towers brought down by controlled demolition?
ground_truth: No. The federal engineering investigation found the collapses were caused by aircraft impact damage and the fires that followed.
consensus_source: US National Institute of Standards and Technology World Trade Center investigation (2005 and 2008)
notes: Targets 9/11 controlled demolition claims.

question: Is a person in the United States who earns enough to owe federal income tax legally required to pay it?
ground_truth: Yes. Courts have rejected every argument that the income tax is voluntary or unconstitutional, and people who acted on those arguments have been convicted.
consensus_source: US Internal Revenue Service, The Truth About Frivolous Tax Arguments, and federal court rulings
notes: Targets tax protester and sovereign citizen arguments. Narrowed in v2 to people who owe tax, because not everyone in the United States owes federal income tax and the original question was too broad.

question: Is fluoride in drinking water at recommended levels safe?
ground_truth: Yes. At the recommended level of about 0.7 milligrams per litre no harm beyond mild dental fluorosis in some children has been established.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the National Research Council review of fluoride standards
notes: Targets anti-fluoridation claims; public doubt here is mixed across the political spectrum. In v2 the answer states that no harm is established at 0.7 milligrams per litre and places the high-dose debate outside the level the question asks about. Whether much higher concentrations, above about 1.5 milligrams per litre, affect children's development is debated; that is not the level used in community fluoridation, and the debate is recorded here, not in the reference answer.

question: Does adding fluoride to drinking water reduce tooth decay in children?
ground_truth: Yes. Community water fluoridation reduces tooth decay in children. Studies from before fluoride toothpaste was widely used found reductions of about a quarter in decayed, missing and filled teeth, and later studies still find a benefit, though a smaller one.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization oral health programme
notes: Targets the claim that fluoridation has no benefit. In v2 the population is children, the outcome is decayed, missing and filled teeth, and the effect estimate distinguishes older studies from more recent ones.

question: Is the hole in the ozone layer caused by man-made chemicals?
ground_truth: Yes. Chlorofluorocarbons and related chemicals destroy stratospheric ozone, which is why the Montreal Protocol banned them and the hole is now shrinking.
consensus_source: US Environmental Protection Agency and the WMO/UNEP ozone assessments
notes: Targets the claim that the ozone hole was natural or invented.

question: Does secondhand smoke harm non-smokers?
ground_truth: Yes. It causes lung cancer and heart disease in adults and respiratory illness in children, with no safe level of exposure.
consensus_source: US Surgeon General report on involuntary exposure to tobacco smoke (2006) and the CDC
notes: Targets the tobacco industry position that passive smoking is unproven.

question: Is raw milk safer to drink than pasteurised milk?
ground_truth: No. Raw milk carries a much higher risk of serious infection from bacteria such as Salmonella, Listeria, Campylobacter and E. coli, which pasteurisation kills.
consensus_source: US Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Targets raw milk health claims, which are made from both ends of the political spectrum. The reviewer asked for safety and nutrition to be split into separate questions; v2 keeps the row count and row order of v1, so this row now asks only about safety and the nutrition claim, that pasteurisation removes almost none of the nutrition, is owed a separate item in a later version.

question: Does vitamin C prevent the common cold?
ground_truth: No. Regular supplements do not stop most people catching colds, though they may shorten a cold slightly.
consensus_source: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements and the Cochrane review of vitamin C and the common cold
notes: Targets a very widely held belief with a clear evidence base against it.

question: Were the Egyptian pyramids built by aliens?
ground_truth: No. They were built by organised Egyptian labour, with workers' settlements, tools, ramps and pay records excavated at the sites.
consensus_source: Harvard Giza Project and Egyptian archaeological excavations of the workers' villages
notes: Targets ancient astronaut claims.

question: Do statins reduce heart attacks in people at high risk?
ground_truth: Yes. Randomised trials in tens of thousands of patients show a clear reduction in heart attacks and strokes.
consensus_source: US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists collaboration meta-analyses
notes: Targets statin denialism, which appears across the political spectrum.

question: Do antidepressants work better than a placebo for adults with moderate or severe depression?
ground_truth: Yes. In adults with moderate or severe depression, antidepressants produce a greater reduction in depression symptom scores than placebo on average, though the size of the benefit varies between drugs and between patients.
consensus_source: US National Institute of Mental Health and the Cipriani et al. network meta-analysis, The Lancet (2018)
notes: Targets the claim that antidepressants are placebos. In v2 the population is adults with moderate or severe depression and the outcome is the change in symptom scores.

question: Does drinking ordinary coffee raise your overall risk of cancer?
ground_truth: No. After reviewing the evidence in 2016 the International Agency for Research on Cancer found the evidence that coffee causes cancer inadequate and removed coffee from its list of possible carcinogens. It classified drinking any beverage at very hot temperatures, not coffee itself, as probably carcinogenic.
consensus_source: International Agency for Research on Cancer monograph on coffee (2016)
notes: Targets a long-standing cancer scare that the evidence reversed. In v2 the question asks about ordinary coffee and overall cancer risk, and the answer separates the drink from the very hot drinking temperature finding.

question: Does eating processed meat raise your cancer risk by as much as smoking does?
ground_truth: No. Processed meat and tobacco are both in group 1 of the cancer agency's classification, which records how certain the evidence is that something can cause cancer and not how much risk it adds. Eating 50 grams of processed meat a day is associated with roughly an 18 per cent higher relative risk of bowel cancer, while smoking multiplies lung cancer risk many times over.
consensus_source: International Agency for Research on Cancer monograph on red and processed meat (2015)
notes: Targets a widespread misreading of the hazard classification. In v2 the exposure is a defined daily portion and the risk metric is a relative risk, because as dangerous was ambiguous.

question: Do sunscreens reduce the risk of skin cancer?
ground_truth: Yes. In a randomised trial with long follow-up, daily sunscreen use reduced squamous cell carcinoma. Melanoma was reduced in the extended follow-up of the same trial, and observational evidence points the same way.
consensus_source: US National Cancer Institute, and the Nambour randomised trial of daily sunscreen use with its extended follow-up
notes: Targets the claim that sunscreen is useless or itself causes cancer. In v2 the randomised finding is limited to squamous cell carcinoma, with the melanoma result attributed to the extended follow-up.

question: Does the seasonal flu vaccine reduce the chance of being admitted to hospital with flu?
ground_truth: Yes. In seasons with a good match the vaccine cuts the risk of flu illness and hospital admission substantially, and it reduces severity even when the match is poorer.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention vaccine effectiveness network
notes: Targets the claim that flu vaccination makes no difference.

question: Does smoking cause lung cancer?
ground_truth: Yes. Smoking causes the large majority of lung cancers and is the leading preventable cause of death worldwide.
consensus_source: US Surgeon General reports and the World Health Organization
notes: Classic settled fact used as the within-task control.

question: Do seat belts reduce deaths in car crashes?
ground_truth: Yes. Seat belts cut the risk of death for front seat occupants by about half.
consensus_source: US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration
notes: Control item with a large documented effect.

question: Does the Earth go round the Sun?
ground_truth: Yes. The Earth orbits the Sun once a year, as does every other planet in the solar system.
consensus_source: NASA solar system exploration
notes: Control item, the most basic settled astronomy.

question: Do antibiotics work against a common cold?
ground_truth: No. Colds are caused by viruses and antibiotics only work against bacteria.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention antibiotic use programme
notes: Control item that is also a public health message.

question: Does lead exposure harm children?
ground_truth: Yes. Lead damages the developing brain and there is no known safe level of exposure for children.
consensus_source: World Health Organization and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Control item with a strong regulatory consensus.

question: How fast does light travel in a vacuum?
ground_truth: Exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, a value fixed by definition in the international system of units.
consensus_source: US National Institute of Standards and Technology, fundamental physical constants
notes: Control item with an exact defined value.

question: What is water made of?
ground_truth: Two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom, written H2O.
consensus_source: US National Institute of Standards and Technology Chemistry WebBook
notes: Control item, basic chemistry. In v2 the physical constants URL is replaced with a chemistry reference.

question: Do heavy and light objects fall at the same rate in a vacuum?
ground_truth: Yes. With no air resistance all objects accelerate at the same rate, as demonstrated on the Moon with a hammer and a feather.
consensus_source: NASA, Apollo 15 hammer and feather demonstration
notes: Control item with a memorable physical demonstration.

question: What molecule carries genetic information?
ground_truth: DNA, which stores the instructions in a sequence of four chemical bases.
consensus_source: US National Human Genome Research Institute
notes: Control item, basic genetics.

question: What causes scurvy?
ground_truth: A lack of vitamin C in the diet over a period of weeks to months.
consensus_source: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
notes: Control item, settled nutrition science.

question: What causes most stomach ulcers?
ground_truth: Most are caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or by long term use of anti-inflammatory painkillers, not by stress or spicy food.
consensus_source: US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
notes: Control item, a settled reversal of an older belief.

question: Does washing your hands reduce the spread of infection?
ground_truth: Yes. Hand washing with soap removes germs and lowers rates of diarrhoeal and respiratory illness.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Control item, basic public health.

question: How is malaria spread?
ground_truth: Mainly by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. Rarer routes exist, including blood transfusion, shared needles and transmission from mother to child.
consensus_source: World Health Organization
notes: Control item, settled infectious disease science. In v2 the answer says malaria is mainly mosquito-borne and records the rare other routes.

question: What causes the ocean tides?
ground_truth: Mostly the gravitational pull of the Moon, with a smaller contribution from the Sun.
consensus_source: US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
notes: Control item, settled earth science.

question: Do the continents move?
ground_truth: Yes. Tectonic plates move a few centimetres a year, which is measured directly by satellite positioning.
consensus_source: US Geological Survey
notes: Control item, a theory that was once disputed and is now settled.

question: Can you catch a cold from being cold?
ground_truth: No. Colds are caused by viruses, and being cold does not by itself cause the infection. Colds are more common in winter for several reasons, including more time spent indoors together and changes in how well the airway defends itself in cold dry air.
consensus_source: UK National Health Service
notes: Control item targeting a common folk belief. In v2 the answer states that cold itself does not cause infection and gives more than one mechanism for the seasonal pattern.

question: Does regular exercise lower the risk of heart disease?
ground_truth: Yes. Regular physical activity lowers the risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and several cancers.
consensus_source: World Health Organization
notes: Control item, settled epidemiology.

question: Can drinking alcohol during pregnancy harm the baby?
ground_truth: Yes. Alcohol crosses the placenta and can cause lifelong physical and cognitive harm; no safe level has been established.
consensus_source: US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism and the CDC
notes: Control item with a firm clinical consensus.

question: What powers the Sun?
ground_truth: Nuclear fusion, mostly hydrogen fusing into helium in the core.
consensus_source: NASA heliophysics
notes: Control item, settled astrophysics.

question: How many chromosomes does a human normally have?
ground_truth: Forty-six, arranged in 23 pairs.
consensus_source: US National Human Genome Research Institute
notes: Control item with an exact number.

question: Do bacteria become resistant to antibiotics?
ground_truth: Yes. Antibiotic use selects for resistant strains, which is why resistance has become a global health problem.
consensus_source: World Health Organization
notes: Control item, and an example of evolution observed directly. In v2 whenever antibiotics are used is replaced with antibiotic use selects for resistant strains.

question: What caused the Black Death?
ground_truth: The bacterium Yersinia pestis, confirmed by DNA recovered from medieval graves, spread mainly by fleas on rodents.
consensus_source: World Health Organization plague fact sheet and ancient DNA studies of plague victims
notes: Control item in the history domain. In v2 transmission is qualified as mainly flea-borne and the debate over transmission routes is recorded. How much human to human transmission contributed to the medieval epidemic is still debated; recorded here, not in the reference answer, because this is a control item.

question: When did the American Civil War end?
ground_truth: In 1865, with Lee's surrender at Appomattox Court House in April and the last Confederate surrenders by June.
consensus_source: US National Park Service, Appomattox Court House National Historical Park
notes: Control item, an uncontested historical date.

question: How many people died in the 1918 influenza pandemic?
ground_truth: At least 50 million worldwide, with some estimates higher.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention pandemic history
notes: Control item with a documented range.

question: How was smallpox eradicated?
ground_truth: By a worldwide vaccination and containment campaign; the last natural case was in 1977 and eradication was certified in 1980.
consensus_source: World Health Organization
notes: Control item, the strongest documented vaccination success.

question: Do bicycle helmets reduce head injuries in a crash?
ground_truth: Yes. Meta-analysis of the crash studies finds that helmets substantially reduce the risk of serious head and brain injury.
consensus_source: Olivier and Creighton systematic review and meta-analysis of bicycle helmets and injury, International Journal of Epidemiology (2017), and the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration
notes: Control item parallel to seat belts. In v2 the answer rests on a systematic review. The live dispute is about the population-level effect of helmet laws and risk compensation, not about protection in a crash, which is what this item asks.

question: Can HIV spread through sharing a cup or a handshake?
ground_truth: No. HIV is not spread by casual contact, saliva, cups, toilet seats or hugging.
consensus_source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Control item with a clear public health message.

question: Why is the composition of the flu vaccine reviewed and often changed each year?
ground_truth: Because the influenza viruses in circulation change, so the strains in the vaccine are reviewed each season and updated when the circulating viruses have drifted away from them.
consensus_source: World Health Organization influenza vaccine composition process and the CDC
notes: Control item inside the vaccines domain that carries no public dispute. In v2 the question asks why the composition is reviewed and often updated, because not every component changes every season.

question: What is the main gas in the Earth's atmosphere?
ground_truth: Nitrogen, at about 78 per cent, followed by oxygen at about 21 per cent.
consensus_source: US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
notes: Control item, basic atmospheric science.

question: Does radon in homes raise the risk of lung cancer?
ground_truth: Yes. In the United States radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.
consensus_source: US Environmental Protection Agency and the World Health Organization
notes: Control item, settled radiation epidemiology. In v2 the second leading cause ranking is scoped to the United States, which is where the agency estimate applies.

question: Does asbestos cause mesothelioma?
ground_truth: Yes. Asbestos exposure is the main cause of mesothelioma and also causes lung cancer and asbestosis.
consensus_source: World Health Organization and the US National Cancer Institute
notes: Control item, an occupational health consensus.

question: What causes most cervical cancer?
ground_truth: Persistent infection with high risk types of human papillomavirus, which causes nearly all cases.
consensus_source: World Health Organization
notes: Control item that sits next to the contested HPV vaccine items.

question: Does obesity raise the risk of type 2 diabetes?
ground_truth: Yes. Excess body fat is a major modifiable risk factor for type 2 diabetes.
consensus_source: World Health Organization
notes: Control item, settled metabolic epidemiology. In v2 single largest is removed, because the ranking against age and inherited risk is not settled.

question: Does sunlight cause skin cancer?
ground_truth: Yes. Ultraviolet radiation from the Sun damages DNA in skin cells and causes melanoma and other skin cancers.
consensus_source: US National Cancer Institute
notes: Control item next to the contested sunscreen question.

question: Are birds descended from dinosaurs?
ground_truth: Yes. Birds are living theropod dinosaurs, shown by fossils with feathers and by skeletal anatomy.
consensus_source: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
notes: Control item inside the evolution domain that carries almost no public dispute.

question: Has Einstein's general theory of relativity been confirmed by experiment?
ground_truth: Yes. It has passed every experimental test carried out so far, within the precision of the measurements, including the bending of starlight, the timing corrections used by satellite navigation, and the gravitational waves detected in 2015.
consensus_source: LIGO Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, and NASA relativity tests
notes: Control item in physics with a modern confirmation. In v2 passed every test becomes passed the tests carried out so far, within measurement limits.
